questions.question: Specific charge of an ion compared with its nucleus
questions.subtopic: Specific charge of an ion compared with its nucleus
questions.prompt: A ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺ ion has an approximate mass of 24.0 u. Assume electron masses are negligible. Use 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Calculate the ion's mass in kg. (b) Calculate the ion's charge and its specific charge in C kg⁻¹. (c) Calculate the nuclear charge and the specific charge of the nucleus. (d) Explain the difference between the two specific charges. [6 marks]
markPoints: Converts 24.0 u to ion mass m=24.0×1.66×10⁻²⁷=3.984×10⁻²⁶ kg.
Identifies the Mg²⁺ ion's net charge as +2e=+3.20×10⁻¹⁹ C.
Computes the ion's specific charge Q/m=3.20×10⁻¹⁹/3.984×10⁻²⁶=+8.03×10⁶ C kg⁻¹.
Identifies the magnesium nucleus charge as +12e=+1.92×10⁻¹⁸ C.
Computes the nuclear specific charge as 1.92×10⁻¹⁸/3.984×10⁻²⁶=+4.82×10⁷ C kg⁻¹.
Explains that the ion retains ten electrons and hence has +2e net charge, while the nucleus is +12e; masses are approximated as the same.
questions.modelAnswer: The approximate mass is m=24.0(1.66×10⁻²⁷)=3.984×10⁻²⁶ kg. The Mg²⁺ ion has a net charge of +2e=+3.20×10⁻¹⁹ C, so its specific charge is Q/m=+8.03×10⁶ C kg⁻¹ (3 s.f.). The nucleus contains 12 protons, so it carries +12e=+1.92×10⁻¹⁸ C and its specific charge is +4.82×10⁷ C kg⁻¹. The ion contains ten bound electrons, reducing its net charge from +12e to +2e. Neglecting electron masses makes the two masses approximately equal, explaining the sixfold difference in specific charge.
questions.questionType: manually assessed multi-step AQA AS Physics numerical working
questions.manualReviewReason: Check two different net/nuclear charges, mass conversion, division and the meaning of specific charge. Do not award automatic marks from isolated numerical tokens.

questions.question: Photon wavelength from an electronic transition
questions.subtopic: Photon wavelength from an electronic transition
questions.prompt: An atom has three electron energy levels E₁ = −13.60 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV and E₃ = −1.51 eV. An electron falls from E₃ to E₂. Use 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the emitted photon energy in eV and J. (b) Calculate the frequency and wavelength of this photon, giving the wavelength in nm. (c) State whether an E₂ → E₁ photon has a longer or shorter wavelength, with an energy-gap reason. (d) Explain why atoms emit only certain photon wavelengths. [7 marks]
markPoints: Finds the E₃→E₂ photon energy as |−3.40−(−1.51)|=1.89 eV.
Converts the energy to 1.89×1.60×10⁻¹⁹=3.024×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Applies E=hf and obtains photon frequency approximately 4.56×10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses E=hc/λ or λ=c/f with the correct photon-energy substitution.
Finds the emitted wavelength λ≈6.58×10⁻⁷ m, equivalent to 658 nm (3 s.f.).
Finds E₂→E₁ energy gap 10.20 eV, which is greater than 1.89 eV, hence that photon's wavelength is shorter.
Explains that discrete electron energy levels allow only specific energy differences and therefore specific photon energies/wavelengths.
questions.modelAnswer: For the drop E₃→E₂, ΔE=|−3.40−(−1.51)|=1.89 eV = 3.024×10⁻¹⁹ J. The frequency is f=E/h=(3.024×10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63×10⁻³⁴)=4.56×10¹⁴ Hz. Using λ=hc/E gives λ=(6.63×10⁻³⁴)(3.00×10⁸)/(3.024×10⁻¹⁹)=6.58×10⁻⁷ m = 658 nm (3 significant figures). For E₂→E₁ the energy difference is 10.20 eV, larger than 1.89 eV, so its photon has a shorter wavelength. Only specific photon energies are emitted because the atom has discrete permitted electron levels.
questions.questionType: manually assessed multi-step AQA AS Physics numerical working
questions.manualReviewReason: Verify level subtraction, the energy in joules, frequency, wavelength units and the inverse relationship with transition energy. These are written calculations, not recall keywords.

questions.question: De Broglie electron diffraction and voltage scaling
questions.subtopic: De Broglie electron diffraction and voltage scaling
questions.prompt: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 150 V, and then passes through a crystal with atomic plane spacing about 0.20 nm. Ignore relativistic effects. Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, electron mass m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy in J and momentum of the electron. (b) Calculate its de Broglie wavelength in nm. (c) Predict its wavelength if the voltage increases to 600 V. (d) Explain why diffraction by the crystal provides evidence of the electron's wave behaviour. [7 marks]
markPoints: Uses energy gained Eₖ=eV=(1.60×10⁻¹⁹)(150)=2.40×10⁻¹⁷ J.
Uses Eₖ=p²/(2m) and rearranges to p=√(2mEₖ).
Calculates the momentum p≈6.61×10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
Uses the de Broglie equation λ=h/p with correctly determined momentum.
Obtains λ≈1.00×10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.100 nm at 150 V.
Explains λ∝1/√V and obtains half the original wavelength, about 0.0501 nm, at 600 V.
States that electron waves diffract when their wavelength is comparable with lattice spacing, and the observed diffraction pattern is wave evidence.
questions.modelAnswer: At 150 V the kinetic energy is Eₖ=eV=2.40×10⁻¹⁷ J. Since Eₖ=p²/(2m), the momentum is p=√(2mEₖ)=√[2(9.11×10⁻³¹)(2.40×10⁻¹⁷)]=6.61×10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. Hence λ=h/p=(6.63×10⁻³⁴)/(6.61×10⁻²⁴)=1.00×10⁻¹⁰ m=0.100 nm. Raising the accelerating voltage from 150 V to 600 V multiplies kinetic energy by four, momentum by two and halves λ to 0.0501 nm. A wavelength of order 0.1 nm is comparable with the crystal's 0.20 nm plane spacing; an electron diffraction pattern therefore demonstrates wave behaviour.

questions.manualReviewReason: Inspect energy conversion, momentum square root and de Broglie calculations, the voltage-scaling argument and the interpretation of diffraction without auto-awarding isolated keywords.
